Kalvarija Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Marijampolės apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. Kalvarija's Jewish community, tracing to the 18th century, built its synagogue in 1713 under a royal condition that it not exceed the height of the local church, and later became so enmeshed in the grain trade with Germany — with merchants living part of the year in Königsberg — that the town's Yiddish developed a distinct, Germanized dialect nicknamed 'Kalvarijer Deitch,' known throughout Lithuania. The town, which peaked at 3,581 Jews (38 percent of the population) in 1897, produced several notable emigrants, including the American congressman Meyer London and Israel Matz, founder of the Ex-Lax company. On August 30, 1941, the entire Jewish community was transferred to the Marijampolė ghetto and, together with Jews from surrounding areas, shot near the town's barracks — 8,600 people killed in total. This cemetery, dating to the 18th century, survived the Soviet period entirely undisturbed and was formally registered in Lithuania's Cultural Property Register in 2015; it sits on a street once informally known as 'Dead Street,' named for the cemetery itself.
